## 1. What was read

**1,220 research articles** from 33 of the 33 journals on the roster.

A further **387** records (24% of the 1,607 this month's harvest returned) carry no abstract and are not research: news, correspondence, editor highlights and obituaries. PubMed types them `Journal Article` and nothing else, so the publication-type filter cannot see them — across the whole index they are 22.7% of it and 35% of `general`, and 3,801 of them are JAMA. Every count below is over the full harvest and is inflated by this; the figure above is not.

!!! warning "Volume swing against the median month: bioinfo +69%, cancer +62%, general +49%, sysbio +104%"
    Check the source before reading anything into this. Two benign causes account for most of these. `bioinfo` every January carries the Nucleic Acids Research database issue and runs high. And several journals simply deposit nothing in some months: across the 44 months read, 4 of 33 journals are absent from at least one, worst being *Nat Mach Intell* (20 months missing, 81 papers in total) and *Bioinformatics* (4 months missing, 2,905 papers in total). Every journal on the roster contributed this month. Queried directly, PubMed returns zero for those journal-months too — the holes are in the source, reproduced exactly by re-running the harvest. So a swing here is not evidence that a field went quiet, and is not usually evidence that the pipeline broke either.

Largest contributors: JAMA 169, Nature 168, Nucleic Acids Res 146, Bioinformatics 145, Science 118, Blood 81.

## 3. The evidence that moved it








*Rewritten 2026-08-26. The first version of this briefing was written from a
single month's reading with no baseline behind it, and several of its statements
could not have been supported at the time. What follows is the same month read
against the eleven months that now precede it.*

!!! note "Corrected 2026-08-27"
    This section opened on "two independent scaling nulls, in the same journal,
    in the same month". There is one.
    [42265212](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42265212/) has no abstract: it is
    the journal's own research highlight of
    [42265208](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42265208/) in the same issue, and
    "much pain with little gain" is the highlight's headline for that paper's
    result, not a second group's finding. The card is now neutral. The argument
    below does not depend on there being two — it depends on the nineteen months
    behind it — but "independent" was the wrong word and the count was wrong.

**A scaling null, and it is the endpoint of a line rather than a break in it.**
[42265208](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42265208/) reports that neither size nor diversity of the
pretraining set buys single-cell foundation model performance;
[42265212](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42265212/), the research highlight alongside it, puts that in a
headline as "much pain with little gain".
Read alone, in July, this looked like the month foundation models broke. Read
against the nineteen-month curve it is the endpoint of a trend that had been
visible for over a year. Simple or linear baselines matching or beating deep
models: [June 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40407144/) (simple controls
exceed the best deep learning for perturbation prediction),
[June 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40434923/) (conservation and solvent
accessibility are almost all you need),
[July 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40605002/) (plain Z-scores
outperform), [July 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40662806/) (sequence-based
interaction predictors plateau at 0.65), then January, May and June 2026. And the
benchmark metrics themselves declared invalid in April, May and June 2026. The
scaling null is not a surprise; it is the last piece of an argument the methods
journals had been assembling since the first half of 2025 — which the corpus
only saw once it read those months.

**And in the same month, the specialized model lost to the general one.**
[42286322](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42286322/) (*Nat Med*) evaluated OpenEvidence and UpToDate Expert
AI against three frontier general-purpose models on 500 MedQA questions, 500
HealthBench items and 100 real physician queries put to a general-purpose model
in a live clinical environment, the last blind-reviewed by 12 US clinicians
across 1,800 annotations. The frontier models won all three, and the clinical
products scored comparably to Google's auto-enabled Search AI Overview. Note
which way that counts. The negative verdict falls on the specialized products;
the finding itself — a broadly trained general model transferring into clinical
use and beating tools built for it — is the foundation-model claim, and this card
supports the thread rather than refuting it. Set against the scaling null the two
point in opposite directions for anyone building: scaling the pretraining corpus
does not help, but the broadly trained general model beats the narrowly trained
specialist. What that combination argues against is the middle — domain-specific
pretraining at moderate scale, which is what most biomedical foundation models in
this corpus are.

**Agentic AI produced a working clinical agent and a benchmark to judge it by.**
[42156546](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42156546/) (*Nature*) automates scientific discovery end to end.
[42310457](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42310457/) (*Nature*) is not the position piece its title
suggests: MIRA is an autonomous agent operating inside a sandboxed electronic
health record, obtaining patient histories, ordering and interpreting laboratory,
imaging and microbiology tests, generating differential diagnoses and formulating
treatment plans down to prescriptions, admissions and scheduled procedures, and
in simulations on real patient cases it outperformed physicians on diagnostic
accuracy while making guideline-concordant, medication-safe admission decisions.
The distinction from the rest of this thread is that it takes structured EHR
actions rather than producing free text. [42412809](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42412809/) is the
benchmark: BAISBench scores AI scientists on cell-type annotation across 15
expert-labelled datasets and on 193 multiple-choice questions drawn from the
conclusions of 41 published single-cell studies, with five graduate-level
bioinformaticians as the human baseline. Its result is two-sided and both sides
matter — the systems fall short of autonomous discovery, and they already show
substantial value in support of it. The maturity signal for this thread has
consistently been the arrival of benchmarks rather than of flagship
demonstrations, and this month has one of each.

**The neuro-immune axis had its best month, and its most mechanistically
specific.** Commensal bacteria [synthesize acetylcholine and use it to instruct
mucosal immunity](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42236946/); nociceptive innervation
[actively suppresses tertiary lymphoid structure formation](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42161272/);
chronic stress [unleashes an intratumoral bacteriophage-fibroblast-B cell
circuit](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42349430/); GABA [drives glioblastoma progression through MDSCs,
sex-dependently](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42337052/). These are the direct mechanistic bridges between
the neural, microbial and lymphoid arms that the thread's claim asserts exist,
and this is the month they arrived together.

**CAR-T against a precursor state.** [CAR-PRISM](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42010117/) puts
ciltacabtagene autoleucel into high-risk smoldering myeloma. Note the tension
with [41380103](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41380103/) five months earlier, which found that genomically
smoldering myeloma is not a distinct entity — the trial is treating a category
the genomics has questioned.

## 4. Refutations

### (a) Landing on a tracked thread

[SKYSCRAPER-01](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42507968/) is the definitive negative phase 3 for tiragolumab
plus atezolizumab in PD-L1-high NSCLC, and [ENHANCE](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42441929/) is the phase 3
failure of CD47 blockade with azacitidine in higher-risk MDS. Two of the class's
largest bets fail in one month.

The corpus's first version of this briefing treated that as the moment the
next-generation checkpoint thesis died. With a baseline it reads differently, and
worse for the thesis: these two failures are the *visible* part of a class that
had already stopped producing candidates. Across all of 2025 not one newly
nominated checkpoint entered a phase 1; October 2025 returned zero hits for the
entire target list; and by December 2025 the new nominations were macrophage
receptors and a long non-coding RNA. The phase 3s did not kill the class. They
were the last readouts of a class that had already stopped replacing itself.

[42276071](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42276071/) (*Immunity*): immunoediting already strips clonal
neoantigens from primary treatment-naive tumours, shrinking the target pool
before any therapy is given. With [41985452](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41985452/), which finds that
neoantigen and immunogenicity prediction models exploit a shared shortcut feature
rather than learning biology, the vaccine thread is attacked on both the target
space and the selection method in one month — while
[42120910](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42120910/) advances a personalized DNA vaccine into
MGMT-unmethylated glioblastoma. Both arms are real; the thread is genuinely
splitting rather than turning.

[42260101](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42260101/) (*Nat Med*): escalating chemotherapy on ctDNA positivity
does not improve disease-free survival in resected colorectal cancer. This is the
escalation arm of the ctDNA-guided paradigm failing. It was previously read
alongside [TOMBOLA](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41544704/) as the second of two failures three months
apart; TOMBOLA met its primary endpoint, so it is not a companion failure and
that pairing is withdrawn. What the two show together is narrower and more
useful: a single-arm trial that starts immunotherapy on ctDNA positivity reports
60% complete response, and a randomised trial that escalates chemotherapy on
ctDNA positivity shows no disease-free survival gain. Detection is not the
problem in either. Which intervention the detection triggers is the whole
question.

### (b) Method credibility

[41985452](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41985452/) is the month's methodological result as well as its
clinical one: two model families that are usually validated separately turn out
to share a shortcut, which means their apparent agreement was never independent
confirmation.

[42260311](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42260311/) (*Nat Methods*) tests sequence-to-function models
against real inter-individual variation — the evaluation these models had been
avoiding, and the one that matters for any clinical use — and reports the result
the card had left out. Training on personal genomes with SAGE-net does improve
expression prediction for held-out individuals, but the gain comes from
identifying predictive variants rather than from learning a cis-regulatory
grammar that generalises across loci. The improvement is real and it is not the
capability the models are sold on.

**Comparability warning.** Several running counts quoted in earlier briefings —
the templated preclinical block, and the foundation-model / frozen-encoder /
generative / agentic tallies — were produced by different readers applying the
same words to different boundaries, and the 2025-01..2025-07 backfill showed the
spread is large enough to invent trends. Those series are recorded in the
briefings that produced them and should not be read across months. The counts
that survive re-reading are the ones anchored to a denominator computed from the
index, not to a reader's judgement.
